subject: Site level density estimates with low occupancy

messages.author: cce2cd493cd35025
messages.subject: Site level density estimates with low occupancy
parts:
I'm using distance sampling to study the effects of several landscape fac=
tors on Northern Bobwhite densities across various sites in North Carolin=
a and South Carolina. We surveyed 148 sites across the two states over t=
he last two summers (2009-2010). Each site was surveyed twice during eac=
h summer.=20=20

I'm using the MCDS engine in Distance to calculate a density estimate at =
site level using the data I've collected. In order to estimate density f=
or each site, I have essentially had to double stratify the data. I have=
classified the percentage forest surrounding each of my sites and classi=
fied each site into a low, medium, or high percent forest class. I've cr=
eated a data filter in distance that selected sites that were within each=
"% forest class". After selecting for a particular % forest class (1,2,=
or 3), I then post-stratified using the sample label (or by each site). =
This essentially allowed me to estimate the density for each site but us=
e the detection probability that was calculated for each % forest class (=
or at the global level).=20=20

So, I calculated an estimate of density for each site but the problem I'=
m running into is I'm getting really high % CVs and wide confidence inter=
vals. Beacuase of the limited number of visits to each site, my observat=
ion numbers of bobwhites per site are low (9 being a high number of obser=
vations for a site over the two summers). I'm pretty sure this is what i=
s causing the high % CVs and wide confidence intervals.

I've heard about some people that are using program R with a bootstrappin=
g method to help with this issue of low observations per site but have be=
en unable to track down any concrete information.

I was interesting to see if anyone else has dealt with this issue, used t=
he bootstrapping method within R or has any other suggestions on how to a=
ttempt to compensate with low numbers of observations.=20=20=20

Thanks,
Shannon Bowling
Master Student=20
North Carolina State University
